title: The shameful and harrowing story of Unit 731
summary: Hosts examine Imperial Japanese Army Unit 731, the secret biological warfare and human experimentation unit that operated in Manchuria in the 1930s and 1940s. They cover the ultranationalist backdrop, the founding under Shiro Ishii, the Pingfan complex and its experiments (vivisection, frostbite, weapons testing, disease dispersal over Chinese villages), the treatment of prisoners of war, and the postwar US deal granting immunity in exchange for data, the Khabarovsk Soviet trial, and the later careers of former members. A listener-mail segment about backdraft closes the episode. Content includes graphic descriptions of atrocities.

segments.title: Content warning and listener sourcing
segments.summary: Hosts warn that the episode covers graphic medical atrocities and thank listener Amy for suggesting the topic.

segments.title: Overview of Unit 731 and comparison to Nazi atrocities
segments.summary: Josh introduces Unit 731 as a Japanese Imperial Army unit whose medical war crimes against Chinese, Russian, Mongolian and other civilians and some POWs rival Nazi medical crimes, and explains that the episode gives context without excusing it.

segments.title: Ultranationalism and Japan's path to war
segments.summary: The hosts describe Japan's late-19th and early-20th century modernization drive, the national humiliation after World War One and the Great Depression, and the rise of ultranationalism in the military.

segments.title: Kwantung Army and Manchuria
segments.summary: The Kwantung Army acted semi-independently to take control of Manchuria, where Japan set up a puppet government in 1932. The region bordered Korea, Russia and Mongolia and was the meeting point of the victims the hosts describe.

segments.title: Founding of Unit 731 under Shiro Ishii
segments.summary: Unit 731 was formed in 1936 under General Shiro Ishii, a doctor and military official interested in biological weapons. He moved operations to lawless Manchuria to avoid scrutiny and to access unwilling subjects.

segments.title: Pingfan complex and its facilities
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Pingfan base, a walled prison-like complex with guard towers where villagers were expelled and staff from medical fields were recruited. Its early mandate was legitimate disease and survival research for soldiers.
topics: Epidemic Prevention and Water Purification Department

segments.title: Shift from soldiers to unwilling civilian subjects
segments.summary: The program moved from consenting soldiers to unwilling prisoners, arrested Chinese civilians and communists, and then toward developing biological weapons. Awareness reportedly reached the top of the government.

segments.title: Biological weapons program and 1925 Geneva Protocol
segments.summary: The hosts say Japan's interest in biological weapons was sparked by the 1925 Geneva ban, and that the program mass-produced pathogens such as malaria, cholera, typhus and plague for testing on human subjects.

segments.title: Vivisection and unanesthetized surgery
segments.summary: The hosts explain vivisection and describe a former Unit 731 doctor's account, reported by Nicholas Kristof of the New York Times, of cutting open a prisoner without anesthesia. Vivisection and amputations were common. Some graphic detail is given.

segments.title: Sexual violence, forced pregnancy and experiments on children and elderly
segments.summary: The hosts describe experiments in which men with venereal disease were forced to rape women, women were impregnated to study fetal effects, babies were born and experimented on, and elderly people were used across a range of ages.

segments.title: Frostbite, blood transfusion and other experiments
segments.summary: Other experiments included frostbite research by Yoshimura Hisato, cow blood transfusions, mismatched blood types, and weapons tests on people. The hosts note the frostbite revival findings are often cited as the only real scientific result, and the second-in-command Kitano said published work attributed results to monkeys.

segments.title: Film recommendation tangent: The Zone of Interest
segments.summary: Chuck recommends the film The Zone of Interest as a way of showing the horror of camp life from the perspective of a commandant's household, and Josh says he will watch it.

segments.title: Pingfan deaths and Hoda satellite site
segments.summary: Pingfan had a satellite site at Hoda about ninety miles from Harbin. Josh says about three thousand people died at Pingfan, with a near 100% mortality rate among prisoners, and that deaths from the broader Manchuria biological warfare program may number in the hundreds of thousands.

segments.title: Destruction of Pingfan and biological attacks on civilians
segments.summary: Survivors were murdered and Pingfan was dynamited before the end of the war, and staff took a vow of silence. The hosts describe testimony from Chinese civilians about dropped grain and disease outbreaks, and the use of infected fleas and dogs.

segments.title: Attacks on prisoners of war and cholera claims
segments.summary: The hosts describe tortured POWs in Singapore, the Philippines and a documented 1945 case involving eight US airmen, and a pathologist's boast about producing enough cholera to kill everyone. They note that the Japanese failed to make the weapons effective.

segments.title: Execution of American POWs after Japan's surrender
segments.summary: Josh recounts a reported incident in which Japanese soldiers beheaded American POWs on a hillside hours after Japan's surrender was announced. Chuck reflects, and Josh notes the Nazis also executed people near the war's end.
topics: war crimes at end of WWII

segments.title: US investigation and immunity deal with Unit 731
segments.summary: After the war, US investigators at Camp Detrick in Maryland questioned former members. Fearing Soviet access, the US chose immunity and payment in exchange for data, and some former scientists advised the US biological weapons program.

segments.title: Douglas MacArthur, John W. Thompson and Nazi versus Japanese prosecutions
segments.summary: Josh contrasts the prosecution of Nazi doctors, led by Canadian John W. Thompson, with the handling of Japanese doctors. The US kept a lid on the story, and MacArthur reportedly called accusations communist propaganda.

segments.title: Yokohama tribunal, Khabarovsk trial and slow disclosure
segments.summary: A Yokohama tribunal in 1948 convicted twenty-three figures for abuses of US POWs and sentences were later reduced. The Soviet Khabarovsk trial in 1949 put twelve members of Unit 731 on trial, and its transcripts were published by John W. Powell in 1982. Japan admitted the program only in 1988.

segments.title: Postwar careers of former Unit 731 members
segments.summary: The hosts describe the later careers of former members: Kitano co-founded Green Cross, whose tainted blood products infected people with HIV in the 1980s and 1990s; Yoshimura became a university president; and Amano Shogo won the Asahi Prize using data from the experiments.

segments.title: Legacy, Fort Detrick questions and Japanese education
segments.summary: Josh says there is no clear evidence the US gained much from the deal, though China accused the US of germ warfare in Korea. Fort Detrick and MK Ultra are mentioned. The hosts note Japan debates teaching this history to children.

segments.title: Listener mail: backdraft
segments.summary: A firefighter listener, Lindsey, clarifies the backdraft explanation from an arson investigation episode, saying a backdraft happens when oxygen is suddenly added to a smoldering, superheated space.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener mail at the show's email address and close the episode.
